source_title: After surviving 85% burns at 21, man helps feed hundreds of US students
source_excerpt: At 21, Joey Brown survived a gas explosion that left burns across 85% of his body, beginning a long and painful journey of surgeries, rehabilitation and learning to perform everyday tasks again. Decades later, he is rebuilding his life in a Georgia high school cafeteria, where he helps care for hundreds of students and has found a community that believes in him. Now, as he looks towards owning a home and welcoming a beagle named Snoopy, Brown says he no longer sees himself as a broken man.A report published by CBS Atlanta documented how Brown, who works at Central High School in Carrollton, Georgia, found renewed purpose through employment and the support of his church. The Georgia Vocational Rehabilitation Agency (GVRA), which helped him secure the job, had previously detailed the long road that brought him back into the workforce.A gas explosion changed his life foreverIn 1988, Brown had recently moved out of his parentsâ home and was sharing an apartment with his brother in Winter Garden, Florida. According to GVRA, he was watching an Atlanta Braves baseball game when he lit a cigarette. The flame ignited fumes from a gas leak, triggering an explosion that knocked him unconscious. When Brown regained consciousness in the apartment complexâs parking lot, a police officer was standing over him and help was on the way. He was airlifted to a hospital in Orlando, where doctors determined that he had sustained severe burns across 85% of his body.The injuries would change nearly every aspect of his life. Brown eventually lost his left arm at the elbow and was left with four fingers on his right hand. His recovery involved repeated operations and a prolonged hospital stay. âIâve had probably 30 to 50 surgeries over the years,â Brown told CBS Atlanta. âI was in the hospital for two and a half years. I had to learn how to walk again and feed myself again.âThe physical injuries were only part of the struggle. For years, Brown found it difficult to face the outside world, conscious of the scars that made strangers stare at him. âFor a long time, I hid from the world. And because of my burns and scars, people would stare at me. But it doesnât bother me no more,â he told CBS Atlanta.Finding a family when he needed oneBrownâs journey back to independence was not something he managed alone. His faith and his involvement with Midway Church in Villa Rica, Georgia, helped him build relationships and find a sense of belonging. He became a greeter at the church, where his willingness to encourage others made him an important presence in the community. Members came to know him not simply as a man who had survived a devastating accident, but as someone who continued to offer kindness despite his own difficulties.âHe is a great, great encourager to many, many people, and they depend on that,â Kay Thompson of Midway Church told CBS Atlanta. Brown said the relationships he developed at church helped fill a deeply felt absence in his life.âI prayed a long time for my own family, and Jesus showed me families every week to come and see me and visit me,â he said. It was through this community that Brown began working towards another milestone: finding a permanent job and becoming more independent.The people who helped him find workAccording to GVRA, Brown first approached the agency for assistance in 2020, but his case did not progress at that time. With encouragement from church member Gerry Herlugson, he reapplied in March 2024 and began receiving vocational rehabilitation services. The agency connected him with Wiregrass Resource Group, a supported-employment organisation, where Kehli Pope became his job coach. Together, they worked towards finding an employer willing to give Brown an opportunity.One unexpected obstacle was the fingerprint-based background check required for school employment. Brown no longer had fingerprints because of his injuries. Pope contacted the school system and helped secure acceptance of a doctorâs note explaining his condition.She also helped him adjust to his responsibilities in the cafeteria, drawing on skills he had already developed while washing dishes at church. âHe washes dishes like a pro,â Pope told GVRA.Brownâs work at Central High School includes operating the commercial dishwasher, disposing of rubbish and helping clean his coworkersâ workstations. After the school year ended in May 2026, he also took a position as an aide in the districtâs summer meal programme. His coworkers have welcomed him as one of their own. Beana Nolley, who works alongside him, told CBS Atlanta that Brown brings energy and warmth to the kitchen. âMr. Joey lights up our kitchen,â she said.Nolley also described how students notice Brown working despite having one arm, using his example to encourage them to believe in their own abilities. For Brown, the job has brought something he had struggled to find after years of uncertainty: a reason to look forward to the next day.âIt makes me look forward to tomorrow because I didnât have nothing to look forward to and give myself hope. And now I got hope from having a job again,â he told CBS Atlanta.A home of his own and a beagle named SnoopyWith employment providing greater stability, Brown has begun looking beyond simply getting through each day. His next goal is to own a home, where he can live more independently and welcome a dog of his own. GVRA reported in July that Brown had been living with his sister for 14 years and hoped to purchase his first home by December 2026. He has been saving towards that goal, while Herlugson has organised a separate fundraiser to help with the down payment.Brown already knows what he wants to call his future companion. âI want to be in my own home by December, so I can celebrate Christmas with my new puppy. My puppy is a beagle. I have decided to name him Snoopy,â he told GVRA.Church members have offered to contribute their time, labour and, in some cases, building materials to help him achieve his dream. Herlugson told CBS Atlanta that the project had become a shared goal for the community.After years in which his injuries and scars shaped how he saw himself, Brown is now looking towards a future defined by his own choices. âI was a broken man now, and Iâm not broken no more,â he told CBS Atlanta.For Brown, the dream is not simply about a house or a puppy.
